progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From skills-s04: assess and evaluate both need a judgement with criteria and evidence; evaluate leans on criteria, assess on how far or how much; memory aid "No verdict without a reason, no reason without evidence." From b12: three biodiversity levels; an effect is a change from a baseline; one variety everywhere narrows genetic diversity. From b13: weigh with conditions; "Verdict, provided that ..."; reversibility. From b19: "Better than what? Shown how? Who gets it?"; released organisms against contained ones. From b16: somatic cell nuclear transfer; the clone matches the nucleus donor, mitochondria come from the egg; low success rates, pregnancy losses; frozen ferret cells returned lost alleles. From b15: count the fathers (alleles come from the breeding animals, not the headcount). From b10: stakeholders; animal welfare; consequences, distribution and principle objections. From b11: how far evidence has got; trials are not proof. Not assumed: xenotransplantation by name (screen only), porcine endogenous retroviruses by name (screen only; spoken "copies of a virus built into the pig's DNA").
progression.startsWith: An unfamiliar biotechnology case and a judgement verb. The video opens: Some of the biggest HSC Biology questions ask you to assess or evaluate a biotechnology.
progression.stopsAfter: assessing the effect of a switch to insect-resistant maize on a district's biodiversity from data (species diversity up compared with sprayed maize; crop genetic diversity down, so the effect is mixed; resistance alleles becoming more common in the pest, an allele-frequency change that threatens the species gain; a verdict to a moderate extent with a checkable condition; the ecosystem level not judged without data); evaluating a plan to clone a rare sheep species from frozen cells (clones of several donors can return lost alleles; donors, not clone numbers, set the gain; mitochondria come from the domestic egg; low success and surrogate welfare costs; breeding management and habitat protection as the alternative, which removes threats but cannot restore lost alleles; a conditional verdict); assessing gene-edited pig kidneys (a large need and a plausible benefit, with early evidence only; costs to the pigs, risks to early patients and a possible virus risk to others; objections in principle; a conditional verdict); recognising a weak answer that describes the organism instead of biodiversity.
progression.nextLesson: why a technology that works scientifically can still have little lasting effect on a population (route entry bio-m6-b20).

teaching.task: When an HSC question asks you to assess or evaluate a biotechnology, how do you turn what you know into a judgement that links the technology to biodiversity, or to the people and animals affected, and back it with evidence from the question?
teaching.causalExplanation: Why sprays falling raises insect species (fewer non-target insects killed, 2c); why fewer varieties is a genetic loss (narrower crop gene pool, one disease could spread, 2c); why rising survivors matter (resistance alleles becoming more common, an allele-frequency change rather than lost diversity; sprays could return and reverse the gain, 2c, 2d); why the alternative cannot replace cloning entirely (breeding and habitat protection cannot restore lost alleles, 3c); why clones of frozen donors can add diversity (each clone carries its donor's alleles, absent from the herd, 3b); why the number of donors, not clones, sets the gain (3b); why welfare costs are high (2 in 100 succeed; many surrogate pregnancies fail, 3c); why cloning alone cannot protect the species (habitat threats remain, 3c); why pig kidneys are not yet proven (few patients, months of function, 4b); why viral copies were inactivated (a virus could spread beyond the patient, 4c).
teaching.conversationalApproach: The biggest HSC Biology questions ask students to assess or evaluate a biotechnology, and markers want the technology linked to its effect on biodiversity or on the people and animals affected, so each walkthrough builds a verdict, criteria and evidence from the question. Q1 (insect-resistant maize) reads the verb as how far, takes the species and genetic levels as criteria against the sprayed-maize baseline, finds a mixed change (fewer sprays raise insect species while fewer varieties narrow the crop gene pool), adds the refuge condition and closes the loop, then sets a weak organism-only answer beside the strong one; Q2 (a cloned wild sheep) evaluates against the three given criteria, with each clone bringing back its donor's alleles, a high welfare cost to the domestic ewes and a conditional verdict; Q3 (kidneys from gene-edited pigs) sizes the benefit against waiting for a human kidney, names who carries each ethical risk and gives a verdict to a moderate extent with its conditions. Q2 and Q3 end with a spoken, crossed classic mistake, and the decision board gives the moves for biodiversity and ethics questions.
teaching.openingDecision: Some of the biggest HSC Biology questions ask you to assess or evaluate a biotechnology. Markers want the technology linked to its effect on biodiversity, not just on the organism, and ethics answers need the same link to the people and animals involved. You have the routine: a verdict, the criteria you judge by, and evidence from the question. Here are three HSC-style questions. Plan each one, then we'll build the answer.
teaching.understandingCheck: Three, each 10 s with the countdown and every demand and condition visible (2a, 3a, 4a). Nothing answer-bearing during the holds; the verdict strip dims.
teaching.curriculumScope: Practice and transfer only; the ledger rows stay with the core videos, and G02 adds practice rows.

design.visualSystem: The skills kit layout (`src/explainer/lessons/skills-shared/`), as in skills-s04: the `QuestionCard` on top (`ZONE.card`) with its annotation layer (`Ann` verb, marks, given, constraint, ring, tag; `CardDim`), the `AnswerBox` below (`ZONE.box`) with margin ticks and a `MarkCounter`, the side column (`ZONE.side`) for plates and the small coded diagrams, and s04's `VerdictStrip` (verdict, criteria, evidence, verdict again) as the mini strip at the far left (`ZONE.strip`), lighting the row each scene builds and dimming to an outline during every countdown. s04's `RoleTag` sits in the answer margin beside each row ("verdict" amber, "criterion" teal, "evidence" ink, "limitation" grey, plus one new tag "condition", amber outline). Q1's mistake scene uses `WeakStrongPanel` (the strong answer moves aside as "Answer B"; the weak answer writes on as "Answer A" with its own counter and a `LostMarksTag`). Each answer row is short (one line, two at most); filled rows dim to grey when the next row writes. When a walkthrough starts, the card shrinks to about 0.7 and each given is underlined in amber in the question text at the cue where it is used (no givens card); a question's type badge ("Biodiversity", "Cloning", "Ethics") stays hidden during each attempt. Earlier questions clear before the next card writes on. Painted plates for real things: `m6-maize-hybrid-rows-v1.png` and `m6-helicoverpa-larva-boll-v1.png` (Q1; the larva plate is shown as "a caterpillar pest", not on maize; see Assets), new `m6-wild-mountain-sheep-v1.png`, `m6-white-sheep-v1.png` (the domestic surrogate) and `m6-insemination-straw-tank-v1.png` (as the frozen cell store) (Q2), new `m6-pig-side-v1.png` and `m8-kidney-nephron-v1.png` (Q3). Coded abstract diagrams only: b12's levels mini-board, a gene-pool ring cluster (b08 and b12 style), a small viral-copy strip, arrows. No people, no hands, no faces; patients and surgeons are never drawn. Never used: `m6-hand-pollination-v1.png` and `m6-agricultural-liming-v1.png` (retired hand plates). Plates scale proportionally, never stretched. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): besides the question strip and the verdict strip, at most about three bright text items in the working area at once; each working tag fades when the next cue lands.
design.transitionPlan: The heading writes on and a word-for-word marking feedback chip writes on "biodiversity"; each question opens on a fresh board with the type badge hidden while the worded card and its data table write, with the maize, wild sheep or pig plate small at its corner; the walkthrough shrinks the card, highlights the verb with its meaning chip and underlines each given in amber as answer rows write with role tags (verdict, criterion, evidence, condition); the refuge strip, the embryo grid and three coded bearer icons build at their cues; the WeakStrongPanel moves the strong answer aside and writes the weak one with its missing roles; each classic mistake writes as a chip and takes a grey scribble cross; the verdict strip returns full size as the three-column decision board, row by row; scene crossfade with settle.

scenes.onScreenChange: board clears. Type badge hidden. New `m6-pig-side-v1.png` sits small at the card's upper left, `m8-kidney-nephron-v1.png` beside it. The card writes on: "Many thousands of people with kidney failure wait years for a kidney from a human donor, and some die while waiting. Scientists have gene-edited pigs so that their kidneys are more suitable for transplant into humans: three pig genes whose products trigger rapid rejection by the human immune system were inactivated, seven human genes that help control immune and clotting reactions were added, and copies of a virus built into the pig genome were inactivated. The pigs are raised in sealed, disease-controlled facilities. Since 2024, a small number of patients have received these kidneys with special permission. Clinical trials of other gene-edited pig kidneys have also begun. One patient's kidney worked for about nine months before it was removed; others are still being followed." Demand: "Assess the use of gene-edited pigs as a source of kidneys for transplant. Refer to benefits and ethical issues. (6 marks)". An eight-line `AnswerBox`, counter "0 / 6".
